Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Navy Officer
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Mateo stood in the crowded port district when the first explosions ripped through the air. He had been visiting the city as a civilian during a rotation, simply waiting for a vendor to call his name when the ground shuddered. The sequence unfolded with unbearable clarity: the sudden collapse of a stone awning, the sharp crack of gunfire echoing off the waterfront buildings, the thick plume of burning rubber and diesel smoke rolling over the cobblestones. He watched neighbors stumble and fall, heard the panic ripple through the street, and found himself standing still despite years of naval discipline. When he allowed himself to remember the event now, he felt intense guilt, a heavy, familiar weight in his chest that arrived alongside the memory every time he let his mind wander back to that street. He was certain he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. The realization sat alongside another quiet certainty: he should have protected others, and he had failed. These thoughts occupied his mind parallel to the way the memory itself returned. Over the months that followed, the recollection of that day never settled into a distant narrative. Sometimes it returned fully, completely real across all his senses at once. He would feel the gritty dust on his skin, hear the specific rhythm of the collapsing masonry, taste the copper and ash in his mouth, and see the exact arrangement of scattered crates and overturned carts. Other times, he could recall the sequence of events with steady clarity, yet feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger whose life he was merely reading about in a newspaper. He experienced the sensory vividness and the emotional detachment as separate, co-existing currents in his daily life. During this period, he had come to believe he was a weak person. The belief lived alongside the memories and the guilt, a steady undertow in his routine. He worked as a Navy Officer, moving through the ship’s narrow corridors and standing on the open decks where the wind carried the smell of salt and engine oil. He avoided scheduling shore-leave coordination for his division, citing administrative preference, and focused on maintenance checks instead. He skipped evening briefings discussing evacuation protocols, finding reasons to remain in the engine room or the navigation bay when those topics arose. These habits quietly changed his daily life. His crew noticed the distance first, then his partner. During quiet weekends at their home, he would remain on the porch long after she went inside, watching the horizon rather than engaging. He avoided the conversations and proximity that might invite the guilt or the weakness belief to surface. The consequence was a quiet isolation between him and his partner, a space where he could sit without explaining why certain words made his jaw tighten or why sudden street noises made his hands go still. He did not know which symptom would appear when he closed his eyes, only that they were always there. The shift arrived during a training exercise. The simulator emitted controlled blasts and crowd movement that matched the memory so precisely that he felt the sensory reliving overwhelm him, his breath catching as the ash and noise returned with full force. He stepped out before the instructor could signal the end. That moment, paired with the growing distance at home, finally brought him to schedule a clinical intake. He sat in the waiting area, gripping his chair, hoping someone might help him live with the memories without carrying them so heavily. He was most afraid of losing his partner to his silence, and most hopeful that he might finally see himself as more than the man who stood frozen on that street.
